content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the offline RL setting in which the data originates from both expert and non-expert sources. The authors suggest that the policy regularization constraints commonly used in offline RL (to stay close to the behavior policy in some way) are not appropriate in this setting and lead to unstable learning behavior. The authors propose two modifications of existing algorithms to deal with this issue, namely a gradient penalty term on the Q-value (Eq 10) and a way to classify and focus the regularization constraint on the expert part of the trajectories (Section 5).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Here are some detailed comments and questions:

For the gradient penalty (GP) technique. The gradients are said to be exploding due to a “failed closeness constraint (OOD actions)”. It seems difficult to make that argument in general scenarios, as that probably depends on the value function and the parametric function used to represent it. The authors illustrate catastrophic failure scenarios (Fig 3) but how do we know these originate from this supposed gradient explosion? 

Question on the gradient penalty: I’m assuming the gradient penalty is optimized with respect to the policy parameters, and not with respect to the critic parameters (which are not mentioned here).

It’s not completely clear why this is the natural form of correction for the supposed problem. The fact that the gradient norm of Q can be upper-bounded under some assumptions (Theorem 4.1) is hardly a justification to bound it to 1 with the penalty term. Could the effect of this penalty term be obtained with a more common entropy regularization on the policy directly?

About the “Constraint relaxation” (CR):

This is motivated by only applying a policy constraint on the expert trajectories, which would require a way to discriminate between expert / non-expert (this isn’t assumed to be known in the data). The learned critic is used to derive a term W(s,a) to modulate the constraint, as a surrogate marker of optimality for a given observed transition in the data. However, the particular formulation chosen doesn’t seem to compute that. For example W could be small in states s which have low Q-values, even though a is optimal (i.e. Q(s,a) = Q*(s,a) but Q(s,a) << Qmax). Wouldn’t using something advantage-based be more appropriate?

The empirical results generally support the effectiveness of the proposed methods for the studied offline RL scenarios (with mixed expert / non-expert data). Though in aggregate existing algorithms like IQL come close. It is not too surprising that algorithms that rely on expert data by assumption fail when provided non-expert data in the mix, but still useful to see these results. The ablation in Fig 8 is useful to understand the separate contributions of GP and CR.

Some more comments:

I’m unsure of the validity of Theorem 4.1 given that it doesn’t seem to assume anything about the smoothness in the transitions (it only assumes smoothness in the policy and the rewards). But what if small changes in the policy lead to vastly different states.

Comment about “Lipschitzness in RL” section: What if enforcing local Lipschitzness in Q is a bad assumption in some MDPs?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing is unclear at times. Some examples:
First sentence in Fig 2 caption: “Non-expert data inhibit in two different ways.”
Fig 2 legend “Policy actions”: which policy? I’m guessing from context it’s the optimized policy.

Figure 6 is hard to interpret. 

Overall, I was able to understand the approach as presented and the writing could be improved with a bit more work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the problem definition makes sense, the approach presented is somewhat reasonable at a high-level, and there is some empirical validation of it in standard continuous-control tasks. I had more trouble grasping the exact arguments and the motivation for the approach chosen in the paper (e.g. justifying Eq 10 based on Theorem 4.1, see other comments above), and I’m unsure about the generality (and therefore scalability) of the approach. content.title: About the GP term
content.comment:
Thank you for your comment. It is very helpful for us to continue to improve this work.
As for your comments about the GP term, we have:

- **the failed closeness constraint (OOD actions).** We agree that the observed failed closeness constraint can be limited to neural networks. We assume that the policy improvement on the expert states (that visited by the expert-level behavior policy) will cause the learned policy decides different actions that far away from the corresponding dataset non-expert actions for non-expert states. Please forgive our temporary inability to prove that this assumption holds when using deep neural network approximators. This assumption is intuitive and is also observed/verified in the middle and right sides of Figure 10 in the Appendix. A counterexample is the tabluar case, where updating a policy for state A does not need to affect the distribution of the policy's actions for state B. 

- **gradient penalty is optimized with respect to ?** Can you please regroup about the second question? (Question on the gradient penalty).
This question seems to have been answered in 'Summary Of The Paper'  (a gradient penalty term on the Q-value (Eq 10) ). In case our understanding is wrong, please consider tell us which part about the gradient penalty term is not clear.

- **Could the effect of this penalty term be obtained with an entropy regularization on the policy directly?**  The proposed gradient penalty term is used to limit the magnitude of the gradient of the Q function with respect to the input actions. Therefore we directly use the form in Equation 10. In addition, there are many ways to restrict the Lipschitz norm of the learned Q-function. We also tested using Spectral Normalisation to limit the magnitude of the gradient of the Q function. It did help prevent catastrophic failures, but also limited the performance (around 20-70). In addition, we also limited the gradient of the Q function w.r.t. the input state on the top of equation 10, but we found that this reduced the performance. These phenomena above support our view that the catastrophic failure comes from the *OOD actions* induced from the policy improvement on non-expert data (i.e., the failed closeness constraint towards non-expert actions).

- **why bound the norm of Q-function gradients (w.r.t. actions) to 1?** Theorem 4.1 is to show that the gradient anomaly of the value function observed in Figure 3 is not reasonable. In order to maintain the properties that the value function should have, i.e., the Lipschitzness, we introduce a one-sided penalty to encourage the norm of the Q-function gradient to remain low in non-expert actions while avoiding excessive penalties for expert actions. 
Why do we choose 1? It's because we don't know what the ground-truth is (and if we did, the real Q-function would be known ). We have empirically found that in some simple tasks, e.g., hopper, changing 1 to 0 brings performance loss. This echoes the hyperparameter study in Figure 11, where a heavy gradient penalty leads to performance degradation.

- **the validity of Theorem 4.1**. We assume the smoothness in the transitions in term $L_{\pi, T}$, as the Jacobian is related to the policy $\pi$ and the environment dynamics $T$. Please consider checking the related discussion in Appendix, page 18.

- **What if local Lipschitzness in Q is a bad assumption in some MDPs?** Thank you very much for this query, and we will add a discussion of this assumption in our next submission. To the best of the authors' knowledge, the iterative solution of the Bellman equation is based on the contraction mapping assumption, which is another form of Lipschitzness (V-function). In addition, in the most extreme case, the gradient of the true Q-function corresponding to any policy should be less than $\frac{1}{1-\gamma} R_{max}$, with $\gamma$ for the discount factor and a mild assumption about the reward $0 \leq r \leq R_{max}$.

content.title: For the Constraint Relaxation (CR) term
content.comment:
For your comments about the CR term, we have:

As you can observe, we only used half a page to introduce CR, as we do not see this as our main contribution. The ablation study also shows that CR only works when the Q function is stable (this can be achieved by GP, in this work). We agree that the advantage-based weight can be better. But we do believe that the Q-value-based weight could serve as a good indicator for the closeness constraints. 

Please consider the toy example that there are two different states $s_1$, $s_2$. For their dataset actions, we have $a_{11}, a_{12}$ and $a_{21}, a_{22}$, respectively. The task of CR is to tell which action is better. We argue that such comparison will only between $\\{a_{11}, a_{12}\\}$ or $\\{a_{21}, a_{22}\\}$, because the closeness constraint is state-wise. One may think the Q-based weight can be false when state $s_1$ has a very low value and thus leads to a very low Q-value for the optimal action (for example, $a_{11}$). However, in this situation, the Q-value for other actions can be lower (e.g., $Q(s_1, a_{12}) < Q(s_1, a_{11})$). And the Q-based weight can distinguish which action is better for state $s_1$ and thus alleviates the harmful closeness constraint.

We agree that the advantage-based weight is better, as it can tell which action is the best among all the dataset actions, and it can avoid the situation of a good action with a low V-value (and thus a low Q-value). But with the state-wise closeness constraint, Q-value-based weight is not a wrong choice. 


Finally, thank you for your professional review and for the time you gave. It is very important for us to further improve this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this work, the authors consider the problem setting of where expert datasets are "contaminated" with sub-optimal data. They identify two issues: 1) OOD actions in states occupied by suboptimal policies; 2) action 'marginalization'/cancelling out over states that are occupied by both expert and non-expert states.

To address issue 1, the authors observe that the learned Q-function should be Lipschitz in actions, so motivate using a gradient penalty that ensures smoothness of the Q-values w.r.t. actions. To address issue 2, the authors propose a value weighted approach for the policy improvement step, which up-weights updates over behavior policy actions in a batch that are optimal according to the critic.

They show on D4RL Locomotion and Adroit tasks that their approach (which they implement on top of BEAR and TD3+BC) is robust to non-expert trajectories compared with approaches that don't explicitly deal with this. They then provide ablations to show that the aforementioned components are key to its success.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The paper is fairly clearly written, and I found it easy to follow the main arguments.
* The proposed methods seem fairly simple, and code is provided to implement them in the Appendix.
* Empirical results seem strong on the proposed problem setting, and resultant "++" approaches seem robust to various degrees of sub-optimal random data.

Weaknesses:
* I find the analysis doesn't necessarily justify the approach, particularly the gradient penalty.
    * The finding that it is in fact OOD actions over the non-expert actions that drive performance degradation is counter-intuitive, especially viewing the right most plot Figure 10; in this case there is greater divergence on the expert actions, yet performance isn't impacted as much. I'd be interested to see this phenomenon examined on more environments (e.g., is it *always* the case that degredation arises to OOD sampling of non-expert data?).
    * Similarly the link between non-expert OOD actions and Q-value action Lipschitzness is not clear to me. There seems to be a leap from "non-expert OOD causes degredation" to "fixing smoothness w.r.t. actions gives great performance". I don't see evidence of the gradient penalty ameliorating the non-expert OOD divergence, and similarly I don't see any analysis of the Q-function action Jacobian as a function of non-expert data mixture amount/performance. Therefore it is unclear to me how one could draw a link between these two observations, and at the moment the smoothness is justified more through "this is a property of well behaved Q-functions". I'd therefore like to see more analysis making the link between these two things clear (e.g., plotting the average norm of the Jacobian with training step). One intuition I could see is that although there is low divergence on expert actions in some cases, the Jacobian around the expert actions could still be high, and this is driven the the OOD estimations on the non-expert data.
    * Doesn't the result in Theorem 4.1 require Lipschitzness in both the underlying reward function and behavior policy? How realistic is this assumption?
    * The constraint relaxation analysis feels lacking. There is brief mention to the didactic illustration in Figure 2, and the left-most plot in Figure 10 doesn't seem to justify their point (indeed, the performance seems rather strong?). While this phenomenom might be well known, some analysis showing that their proposed weighting approach works in the way they intend would be welcomed.
* I'm not entirely convinced by the BC results, particularly filtered BC. Looking at the results in [1], it seems using just the top 10% of data can achieve superlative results. Perhaps the authors could clarify why their %BC results are so much worse than [1], as this would present a very strong baseline?
* I would also appreciate results on replay datasets. While the authors argue this data are less realistic, and may have lower OOD actions, I would still expect to see their approach benefit, especially since TD3+BC seems to struggle on these datasets.

[1] Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning, Kostrikov et al., ICLR21
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work overall seems good quality, and I found the paper easy enough to parse. The novelty isn't significant (gradient penalties and weighted updates have both been discussed in the offline RL context before, e.g., Fisher-BRC, CRR), but the approach seems simple and effective for the problem setting proposed. I'd like to see a promise of the datasets and codebase being released.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper discusses an interesting problem setting and is fairly clear, but I have reservations regarding some of the analysis and the empirical results (specifically %BC performance). Therefore I'd be reluctant to recommend acceptance unless these have been addressed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer uDh8
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your professional review, for your concerns, we have:

**The phenomenon in Figure 10** 

Thank you for checking the appendix. Figure 10 is used to illustrate: 
* (the most left one). The harmful closeness constraint happens on the policy constraint-based methods with expert-medium alike datasets. It shows that the closeness between the learned policy and the random dataset actions (from the random-level behavior policy) is also constrained. This is harmful to policy improvement as non-expert and expert states show great overlaps (Figure9). 
* (the middle and the most right subplot). The failed closeness constraint happens with (after) the policy improvement. The policy improvement means that the learned policy generates actions that are similar to the expert data actions. In Figure 10, this can be verified by the reduced divergence between the policy action and the ‘dataset expert actions’ in the initial phase. We visualized the failed closeness constraint (the enlarged divergence between the policy decisions and the non-expert actions). 
* For the counter-intuitive finding that the policy actions are closer to the non-expert actions, this does not imply a bad policy or a lousy learning process. Because the non-expert states can be far away from the expert ones.

**The link between the GP term and the non-expert trajectories.**

In this work, we find the policy improvement on expert data may lead to failed closeness constraint (Figure 10), thus, OOD actions and a large concentrability coefficient. With Theorem 3.1, we show that this can lead to unstable Q estimations. Prior work handles OOD actions by penalizing the Q-values or enforcing the closeness. Our finding is that the OOD actions can also influence the learning process by extreme sharpness of Q-values w.r.t. actions (Figure 3). We motivated the gradient penalty term by proof that the well-behaved Q-function should be a Lipschitz function (Theorem 4.1).

The average norm of the Jacobian with training step is provided in Figure 3, where the magnitude of Q-function w.r.t. input random actions exceeds 1e5 for the contaminated datasets.


**The assumption in Theorem 4.1** 

We apologize for the misleading term $L_{\pi,T}$ in Theorem 4.1. Please check the discussion about it on page 18. Theorem 4.1 requires Lipschitzness in the underlying reward function, behavior policy, and dynamics.

To the best of the authors' knowledge, the iterative solution of the Bellman equation is based on the contraction mapping assumption, which is another form of Lipschitzness (V-function). In addition, in the most extreme case, the gradient of the true Q-function corresponding to any policy should be less than $\frac{1}{1-\gamma} R_{max}$, with $\gamma$ for the discount factor and a mild assumption about the reward $0 \leq r \leq R_{max}$. 

**The constraint relaxation lacks analysis** 

As you can observe, we only used half a page to introduce CR, as we do not see this as our main contribution. The left-most plot in Figure 10 is a TD3BC agent, and its performance is about 101, which is lower than that trained on the expert dataset (Table 1). 

**The results of BC**

The current BC results are generated from a simple deterministic agent with MSE loss, and its performance is close to the records in the TD3+BC paper. The results from the IQL paper seem to be from a trajectory-based %BC (a stochastic policy with KL loss). We rerun our BC agent in the same trajectory-based dataset filtering setting. Please check the results in the revised version.

**Results on replay dataset**

Please check the results in the revised version, Table 8, on the last page in the appendix. The proposed technique is not designed for medium-replay datasets (maybe we should change the title next time). We empirically find that the proposed techniques help the BEAR agent recover to medium-level performance. But for the TD3BC algorithm, the boosting is not significant.

This reflects the limitation of our work. That the proposed gradient penalty plug-in is designed to stabilize the learning process by suppressing the unstable sharp Q-functions induced by OOD actions generated from the policy improvement step on dataset non-expert states. The replay datasets record decision behaviors from random to near-expert policies for each dataset state. Thus the probability of generating OOD actions during the policy improvement steps is much smaller for the replay dataset.

---
Finally, we want to say thank you again for your professional review and for the time you gave.

content.title: Thanks!
content.comment:
Thanks for your reply, and for running the additional experiments in Table 8.

I still believe the claims in the paper are too strong; concretely, it seems the argument is that random actions have a "knock-on effect" on the value smoothness around *expert* actions, which causes extrapolation errors when learning an actor. However, Figure 3 shows Jacobians around all actions, not just expert actions. Perhaps the expert action Jacobians are well-conditioned, and the relative increase is driven by the sharpness around random actions. Furthermore the theorem seems orthogonal to this claim, and not that useful; in short, assuming MDP related properties (rewards, dynamics, etc.)  are smooth, it's fairly obvious to assume that the value function should be smooth too. It's unclear if the MDPs considered here actually have these properties.

Regarding the explanations in Figure 10, it seems my concern in the rightmost subfigure are still not addressed; there's an assumption that this paradox is explained by the lack of shared support between expert and non-expert states, but no evidence is provided for this.

The authors should also consider backing up their claims with additional mechanisms for ensuring smoothness. For instance, do spectral norms [1] also have a similar benefit on OOD extrapolation?

Finally, I was not aware that BRAC+ also employs a similar gradient penalty. Therefore they key novelty in this work is the insight surrounding this smoothness "knock-on effect" described above, but I feel this is still not strong enough for the reasons stated above. Also I find the lack of analysis around CR still concerning. The authors claim isn't a main contribution, but it is clearly mentioned in the abstract itself.

[1] Spectral Normalization for Generative Adversarial Networks, Miyato et al., ICLR18

content.title: Repsone to Reviewer uDh8
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your views. It will help us to continue to improve this work.

For the evidence of 'lack of shared support between expert and non-expert states', please check the visualization in Figure 9, where we find there are different state overlaps in different contaminated dataset settings.

For the effect of SN, we apply it to the learned Q-function to check whether SN could replace the role of GP. Following the advice from the SNRL paper, we apply it to the layer before the output layer. The results are:

|          | Expert | Medium-expert | Eexpert-random-10 | ER-30 | ER-50 |
|----------|--------|---------------|-------------------|-------|-------|
| TD3+BC   | 104.5  | 101.6         | 98.8              | 14.2  | 8.6   |
| TD3BC+SN | 88.9   | 98.5          | 91.6              | 64.1  | 33.9  |
| TD3BC+GP | 99.8   | 89.1          | 98.5              | 104.0 | 101.4 |

The SN technique could alleviate the catastrophic failure issue in the ER3 and ER5 settings, where the Q-function gradients tend to be sharp. However, its effectiveness is not as well as the GP's.

We think two elements can result in this. Firstly, SN forces the Lipscthizness constant to be 1, w.r.t. both input actions and input states. While in our setting, there seems no reason to penalize the norm w.r.t. input states. Another reason might be the choice of the layer. SNRL paper says it is best to apply normalization to the layers with the largest weight. Thus, they apply SN on the layer before the output layer. But in the offline RL setting, this consumption might be wrong. 

We agree that the key novelty in this work is the insight surrounding the exploding Q-function gradients, and we will continue to improve in this area.

---
Thank you again for sharing your perspective.

content.title: Response to Reivewer XqZa
content.comment:
Thank you for pointing out the lacking of a literature review. We will include them in our next submission.

Please condiser telling us which paper also takes the same setting as ours for the contaminated dataset. To the best of our knowledge, there are many similar settings such as ‘noisy demonstrations[1]’, ‘heteroskedastic data[2]’, and ‘mixed datasets[3]’. But our setting is more comprehensive and more open-source friendly (only a slight modification of the replay buffer is required). 

We cannot agree with the comments that ‘non-expert trajectories can destroy the Q-function via OOD actions’ is well known. In this work, we visualize two ways that non-expert data inhibit policy improvement, in Figure 2 and detailed in Figure 10. The first way (the harmful closeness constraint towards non-expert dataset actions) has also been discussed in the concurrent work [2]. The second way (the failed closeness constraint induced by policy improvement on non-expert data) can be verified by the exploding Q-value and Q-gradients. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to find that OOD action causes not only high Q-values but also sharpness Q-functions (Figure 3.). Please consider citing some papers. 

[1] Behavioral Cloning from Noisy demonstrations. https://openreview.net/forum?id=zrT3HcsWSAt

[2] Offline Reinforcement Learning from Heteroskedastic Data Via Support Constraints. https://openreview.net/forum?id=Rg1LG7wtd2D

[3] Reducing Conservativeness Oriented Offline Reinforcement Learning. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.00098.pdf

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an offline RL algorithm for contaminated datasets where the datasets contain expert-level trajectories and suboptimal trajectories. The proposed methods are built upon policy-constrained offline RL algorithms, where two components are additionally introduced: First, the gradient penalty to the critic network, and second, state-action-dependent behavior regularization that encourages staying close to the dataset action for high-Q samples and vice versa. Experimental results show the effectiveness of adding these components (TD3BC++ and BEAR++), outperforming baselines in contaminated datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]
1. The proposed method is simple to implement yet significantly improves the existing policy-constrained offline RL methods in the contaminated datasets.
2. The paper is easy to follow and the proposed method is well-motivated by providing some empirical observations.


[Weaknesses]
1. The algorithmic novelty is limited. The gradient penalty to the value network has already been introduced in previous works, e.g. [1,2]. The idea of adaptive behavior-regularization for each sample is also not new, e.g. [1,3], though the detailed implementation is different.
2. Theorem 4.1 may be wrong. I think the Lipschitz continuity for the value function cannot be proven without the assumption of the Lipschitz continuous 'transition' dynamics. Intuitively, for example, if the deterministic next state transition is abruptly changing at some action $a$ (e.g. due to obstacles/walls in a specific direction), the value function should also be abruptly changed. However, the current statement of the theorem does not reflect this at all. The proof for Lipschitz continuity on the value function has been provided in [4] with the assumption about both the reward and transition functions.
3. The proposed constraint relaxation (CR) seems to be a heuristic method, rather than a principled approach. It would be great if theoretical justification can be provided.
4. The performance of %BC should be better if we select the top X% of 'trajectories' based on the episode return, rather than using the top X% of 'transitions' with high immediate rewards. We're dealing with sequential decision-making, and thus trajectory-based dataset filtering would be much more natural. Besides, according to the reviewer's personal experience, performing BC on only 100 expert trajectories was usually enough to recover the expert performance. That being said, the trajectory-based %BC for the ER1 dataset will use 100 expert trajectories, and it can recover the expert performance well.
5. This paper assumes that the dataset is a mixture of 'expert' trajectories and suboptimal trajectories, where this assumption may be strong and not be satisfied in many realistic scenarios where the optimal policy is unknown. I am curious to see the performance of the proposed method in more diverse dataset settings such as medium or medium-replay in d4rl. Do TD3BC++ and BEAR++ still outperform the baselines even when using those datasets that do not contain expert trajectories?


[1] Lee et al., Batch Reinforcement Learning with Hyperparameter Gradients, ICML 2020, http://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/lee20d/lee20d-supp.pdf

[2] Zhang et al., BRAC+: Improved Behavior Regularized Actor Critic for Offline Reinforcement Learning, ACML 2021, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.00894.pdf

[3] Xu et al., Offline Reinforcement Learning with Soft Behavior Regularization, 2021, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.07395.pdf

[4] Asadi et al., Lipschitz Continuity in Model-based Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.07193.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and easy to understand. Still, the technical novelty is limited since similar approaches have been proposed in the existing works.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work introduces two simple modifications to the policy-constrained offline RL algorithms and shows promising empirical results on the contaminated (expert+suboptimal) datasets. However, the technical novelty is limited and the theorem seems to be wrong. Also, the experiments can be strengthened by adding the results of the trajectory-based %BC and the results of the more diverse dataset settings such as medium and medium-replay.

content.title: Response to Reviewer k7Qs
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive comments. For your concerns, we have:

**The algorithmic novelty is limited.** We agree that the gradient penalty technique has been shown in prior work. But why use the gradient penalty is the most important. This work finds that policy improvement on non-expert actions leads to OOD actions and **exploding Q-function gradients w.r.t. input actions**. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first to find that OOD action causes not only high Q-values but also sharpness Q-functions (Figure 3.). This motivates the GP term.

We greatly appreciate your comments on the related work. And we'll include them in our next submission.

**Theorem 4.1 may be wrong.** We apologize for the misleading term $L_{\pi, T}$ in Theorem 4.1. Please check the discussion about it on page 18. We achieve Theorem 4.1 with Lipschitzness assumptions in the underlying reward function, behavior policy, and dynamics.

**CR should be supported.** 
We only used half a page to introduce CR, as we do not see this as our main contribution. We agree with you that we should give CR more analysis. 

**The performance of %BC.** 
We rerun our BC agent in the same trajectory-based dataset filtering setting. Please check the results in the revised version. We split the trajectories by two metrics: 1. the difference between the next_state[i] and state[i+1], 2. and the done[i] from the transitions. 


**Other diverse dataset settings without expert demonstrations.** We run TD3BC and TD3BC++ on walker2d-medium-random datasets, which are similar to the expert-random but replace the expert demonstration with medium-level trajectories. We observed the sharp Q-function gradients and the catastrophic failures. And this can be saved by the GP term. Please check the results in the following table.

|               | Walker2d-medium-random-10 | Walker2d-medium-random-30 | Walker2d-medium-random-50 | Walker2d-medium-random-70 |
|---------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| TD3+BC        | 43.5                      | 36.6                      | 17.9                      | 18.9                      |
| TD3BC++(ours) | 71.5                      | 77.1                      | 76.7                      | 74.8                      |

For the results on the replay dataset, please check them in the revised version, Table 8, on the last page in the appendix. The proposed technique is not designed for medium-replay datasets (maybe we should change the title from ‘taming … for non-expert demonstrations’ to ‘taming ... for contaminated dataset’). We empirically find that the proposed techniques help the BEAR agent recover to medium-level performance. But for the TD3BC algorithm, the boosting is not significant.

---
Finally we would like to say thank you for your professional review, your comments will help make this work better.

Thanks again to the four reviewers for their help.
